stories.title: The Shs 2.4 trillion question Parliament cannot postpone
stories.deck: A supplementary spending request has reopened an old argument about how Uganda counts its money — and who gets to see the books.

body.text: For three hours on Tuesday, the finance committee room carried the familiar rhythm of a budget hearing: a thick document, a row of officials, and questions that arrived faster than the answers.

The request on the table is for Shs 2.4 trillion in supplementary expenditure. On paper it is a housekeeping exercise — money already committed, moved from one line to another, signed off before the financial year closes. In practice it is the clearest test yet of whether Parliament can follow money it did not spend itself.

Officials from the Ministry of Finance told the committee that Shs 1.3 trillion of the request covers arrears to suppliers and contractors, with the balance going to security operations, road maintenance and a top-up for the health sector. The committee's chair, however, returned repeatedly to a single annexure: a list of 41 projects whose original budgets were revised twice inside nine months.

text: You cannot ask us to approve an amendment to an amendment and call it transparency.
Committee chair, speaking at the hearing

body.text: Where the money goes

The largest single line is Shs 610 billion for works and transport, most of it for road rehabilitation in districts that have already exhausted their maintenance budgets. Health takes Shs 288 billion, including arrears owed to two regional referral hospitals, while the security vote rises by Shs 174 billion.

items: Works and transport — Shs 610bn, chiefly road maintenance arrears
Health — Shs 288bn, including supplier debts at regional hospitals
Security — Shs 174bn for operations and equipment
Water and environment — Shs 96bn for flood response in the east

body.text: Officials argue the pace is a consequence of a difficult year: a weaker shilling in the first quarter, higher fuel prices and a slower-than-expected collection rate all pushed spending beyond original projections. The supplementary, they say, is the mechanism finally catching up with reality.
A Parliament playing catch-up

Critics of the process say the problem is not the arithmetic but the sequence. By the time a supplementary reaches the floor, the money has usually been spent; the vote is a ratification, not a decision. The committee has asked for quarterly reporting on every line above Shs 5 billion, a request that has been made, and quietly dropped, in each of the last four financial years.

The House is expected to debate the request next week. What the debate produces — a cleaner annexure, a firmer reporting rule, or simply a vote — will say a great deal about how this Parliament intends to be remembered.

For the traders in Kikuubo, the hospital administrators in Gulu and the contractors still waiting on last year's certificates, the question is more concrete. Money that moves between budget lines is money that has not yet moved through their hands.

stories.image_caption: Finance officials appear before the budget committee in Kampala on Tuesday.

stories.title: City Hall moves to reclaim the pavements. The traders are not moving.
stories.deck: A week after enforcement teams cleared the walkways of Kikuubo, a fragile standoff has settled over the city's busiest trading streets.

body.text: At 7am on Wednesday, Betty Namusoke had already rebuilt her stall. By 9am, two enforcement officers had asked her to take it down. By noon, she had rebuilt it again, three metres further from the kerb, and carried on selling tomatoes.

That loop — clear, rebuild, negotiate — has defined the week since the city authority announced a renewed push to reopen pedestrian walkways in the central business district. Officials describe the exercise as a safety measure, citing two fatal accidents involving pedestrians forced onto the road.
Traders describe something else: a familiar cycle in which they are moved without notice to a market they cannot afford, and return because the rent is impossible and the customers are here.

text: I have paid for a stall at the market. It is empty, because nobody walks there. My customers walk here.

body.text: A market built for fewer people

The dispute is not new. Kampala's designated markets were planned for a smaller, more formal retail economy. The vendors who sell on the street today — an estimated 40,000, according to a traders' association — were never allocated space in them.

City officials say a compromise is being drafted: timed trading zones on four streets, with a 6pm cut-off and a daily levy. Traders' representatives say they have heard that promise before, and want it in writing before they move a single crate.

stories.image_caption: Evening traffic on a central Kampala street this week.

stories.title: Cabinet approves digital identity roadmap after two-year delay
stories.deck: The plan would link national identification to mobile money, health records and school enrolment — raising questions about consent and cost.

body.text: Cabinet has approved a long-delayed roadmap for a national digital identity system, setting out how a single identifier would be used across public and private services over the next five years.

The document, seen by UnderCover, proposes a phased rollout beginning with mobile money registration and health records, followed by school enrolment, land titles and tax registration. A pilot in twelve districts is expected before the end of next year.

Supporters argue that the current patchwork of registers wastes money and excludes the poorest citizens from services that require proof of identity. Critics worry about a system that becomes impossible to opt out of.
Consent, cost and the long tail

The roadmap includes provisions for data minimisation and an independent oversight board, but does not specify how citizens could correct errors, a recurring problem with the existing register. It also leaves the funding question open beyond the pilot phase.
Civil society groups have asked for the full text to be published before the pilot begins. Officials say publication will follow parliamentary review.

stories.image_caption: Developers at a Kampala technology hub. The roadmap envisages a single digital identity layer.

stories.title: Teachers suspend strike after pay talks breakthrough
stories.deck: Unions say a phased salary adjustment will begin in January. Head teachers warn that term dates leave little room for recovery.

body.text: Teachers' unions have suspended a planned nationwide strike after reaching an agreement with the education ministry on a phased salary adjustment beginning in January.

The deal moves the lowest-paid teachers onto a revised scale in the first quarter, with a second tranche promised in the next financial year. Unions describe it as a first step; the ministry describes it as the limit of what the current budget can carry.
Head teachers say the practical problem is time. Two weeks of teaching have already been lost in some districts, and end-of-term examinations are fixed.
The agreement will be reviewed in April, when the next budget framework is tabled.

stories.image_caption: A busy trading street in Kampala. Public sector pay talks concluded on Tuesday.

stories.title: Flood warnings issued for eastern districts as river levels climb
stories.deck: Emergency teams are pre-positioning supplies in six districts after a week of heavy rain upstream.

body.text: Authorities have issued flood warnings for six eastern districts after river levels rose sharply following a week of heavy rain upstream.
Emergency teams are moving food, water treatment tablets and temporary shelter to staging points. Schools in low-lying areas have been asked to prepare alternative arrangements.
The warnings come as meteorologists forecast continued rainfall through the first week of November. Communities along the flood plain have been advised to move livestock to higher ground.

stories.image_caption: Low-lying settlements along the city's drainage channels are also at risk.

stories.title: Cholera cases confirmed in three border towns
stories.deck: Health teams have set up treatment units and are tracing contacts after cases were reported at crossings with two neighbours.

body.text: The health ministry has confirmed cholera cases in three border towns, prompting the activation of treatment units and a contact-tracing exercise.

Officials say the cases are linked to unsafe water sources at busy crossings where sanitation is limited. Chlorination points have been installed and health workers are conducting house-to-house checks.
The ministry has urged travellers to carry treated water and to report symptoms early. Stocks of oral rehydration salts are being replenished in the affected districts.

stories.image_caption: Clean water points are being established in the affected towns.

stories.title: Court orders fresh audit of district road contracts
stories.deck: Judges found that procurement records for 14 contracts were incomplete, and asked the auditor general to reopen the file.

body.text: The High Court has ordered a fresh audit of 14 district road contracts after finding that procurement records were incomplete and, in several cases, could not be produced at all.
The ruling follows a petition by a local civil society group that spent two years requesting contract documents under the access to information law.
The auditor general's office has been asked to report within 90 days. Payments on the contracts have been suspended in the meantime.

stories.image_caption: A road under repair on the city's northern edge.

stories.title: Coffee exports hit a record. The farmer's share has not followed.
stories.deck: A strong crop and firm prices have lifted earnings to an all-time high, but growers say the gains stop at the first buyer.

body.text: Uganda's coffee exports have reached their highest value on record, driven by a strong robusta crop and firm international prices. The headline number is, by any measure, a good one.

The number that matters to growers is smaller. Farm-gate prices have risen, but by far less than the export value, because the cost of the middle of the chain — transport, processing, financing and a dozen layers of buying — has risen faster.

At a buying centre outside Mityana, a farmer with two acres described the arithmetic simply: fertiliser cost more this year, labour cost more, and the price he was offered moved by a fraction of what he read in the newspaper.
The long middle

Economists point to consolidation further up the chain, where a small number of exporters handle a large share of volumes, and to the cost of credit for cooperatives that want to hold stock and sell later.
Cooperatives that have tried do better. One union in the west now processes and exports directly, paying members a second payment after sale. It handles a rounding error of national volume — for now.
For the industry, the record is a platform. Whether it becomes a floor for growers depends on the part of the chain that never makes the press release.

stories.image_caption: A trader sorts beans at a buying centre in central Uganda.

stories.title: Mobile money agents push back on new float caps
stories.deck: Agents say tighter limits will push customers back to cash. Regulators say the rules target a specific kind of risk.

body.text: Mobile money agents have asked the central bank to review new caps on agent float, arguing that the limits will force customers back to cash in areas with few bank branches.

The rules, phased in this quarter, require agents to hold balances within set bands and to report large transactions in real time. Officials say the aim is to reduce the risk of fraud and of agents operating as unlicensed deposit takers.
Agents counter that the reporting requirement assumes reliable connectivity that many rural outlets do not have.
A review meeting is scheduled for next month.

stories.image_caption: A mobile money counter in the city centre.

stories.title: Shilling steadies as the central bank mops up liquidity
stories.deck: Traders describe a calmer week after a volatile October, with importers still cautious.

body.text: The shilling has steadied against the dollar after a volatile start to October, helped by central bank operations to absorb excess liquidity.
Importers remain cautious, with several delaying non-essential orders until the direction of the market is clearer. Exporters have taken advantage of the weaker rate to convert earnings.
Analysts expect the currency to trade in a narrow band through November, barring a sharp move in oil prices.

stories.image_caption: Banking district, Kampala.

stories.title: Ntinda tech hub opens with 200 desks and a waiting list
stories.deck: The workspace is the largest of its kind outside the city centre, and its founders are betting on the suburbs.

body.text: A new technology hub in Ntinda opened this week with 200 desks, a recording studio and a small fund for early-stage teams.
Its founders argue that the next wave of Ugandan startups will be built in the suburbs, where rent is lower and the commute is shorter, rather than in the towers of the city centre.
The waiting list for desks already runs to three months. The hub plans to add a second floor next year.

stories.image_caption: Developers at work in the new Ntinda space.

stories.title: Boda riders test electric bikes as fuel costs bite
stories.deck: A pilot in three divisions offers battery swaps on credit. Riders are doing the maths on range and repayment.

body.text: Fifty riders in three city divisions are testing electric motorcycles under a pilot that includes battery swapping and a repayment plan tied to daily earnings.
For riders, the appeal is arithmetic: a full charge costs a fraction of a tank of petrol. The hesitation is range, charging time and what happens when a battery fails on a bad day.
The pilot's operators say swap stations will be expanded if repayment rates hold above 90 percent.

stories.image_caption: A rider on a central Kampala street.

stories.title: Informal traders form a cooperative to buy wholesale
stories.deck: Nine hundred vendors have pooled deposits to negotiate directly with suppliers, cutting out two layers of middlemen.

body.text: Nine hundred market vendors have registered a cooperative that pools weekly deposits to buy stock directly from suppliers, bypassing two layers of intermediaries.
Organisers say members have cut their cost of goods by between eight and fifteen percent in the first month. The cooperative now plans to lease a warehouse.
The model depends on trust and record-keeping, both of which have sunk similar efforts before.

stories.image_caption: Vendors at a produce market in Kampala.

stories.title: Cranes edge Zambia in a five-goal thriller under the lights
stories.deck: A stoppage-time header settled a match that swung four times and left Namboole hoarse.

body.text: For eighty-nine minutes this was a match about nerves. Then a corner from the left found a head at the near post, and Namboole made a noise that could be heard from Kireka.
Uganda had led twice and been pegged back twice. Zambia's equaliser on the hour was the better goal of the five; the winner was the more important.
What it means

The result leaves the Cranes second in the group with two fixtures to play, and in control of their own qualification. The coach, though, was careful afterwards: two matches, he said, is a long time in a group this tight.

text: We won the second ball all night. That is not luck, that is work.

body.text: Attention turns to next month's away fixture, where a point may be enough. On this evidence, nobody in the dressing room is planning for a point.

stories.image_caption: Uganda's forward strikes during the second half at Namboole.

stories.title: Kampala City go top after an 89th-minute winner
stories.deck: A scrappy game turned on a substitution and a moment of impatience from the visitors' captain.

body.text: Kampala City moved to the top of the table with a 1-0 win that will not appear on any highlight reel but may be remembered in May.
The visitors had the better of the first hour and missed three clear chances. City's manager changed shape, pushed a winger inside, and got his reward in the 89th minute.
The result leaves City a point clear with a game in hand.

stories.image_caption: Kampala City celebrate the late winner.

stories.title: Nakato breaks the national 10,000m record in Nairobi
stories.deck: The 23-year-old took eleven seconds off a mark that had stood for nine years, then apologised for not going faster.

body.text: Prossy Nakato broke the national 10,000m record in Nairobi on Sunday, taking eleven seconds off a mark that had stood since 2017.
She ran the second half of the race alone after the pacemakers dropped out, and still closed with a 68-second final lap.
Her coach said the target now is the world championships qualifying standard, which she is within four seconds of.

stories.image_caption: Distance runners at the national trials earlier this year.

stories.title: Onyango signs with a Nairobi promoter and eyes a continental title
stories.deck: The unbeaten welterweight says the move gives him the fights he could not get at home.

body.text: Unbeaten welterweight Samuel Onyango has signed a three-fight deal with a Nairobi promoter, with a continental title shot pencilled in for February.
Onyango, 26, has stopped nine of his fourteen opponents. His team says the move was about access to ranked opponents rather than money.
His first outing under the new deal is expected in December.

stories.image_caption: Onyango during a training session in Kampala.

stories.title: Sevens squad named for the Africa Cup with three uncapped players
stories.deck: A youthful forward pack will face a difficult pool in Accra, where Uganda defend a title they won in 2024.

body.text: Uganda have named a 14-man sevens squad for the Africa Cup in Accra, including three uncapped players in the forward pack.
The team defends a title won two years ago, and opens against a physically imposing pool that includes the hosts.
The coach said the selection reflects a two-year plan rather than a single tournament.

stories.image_caption: The national sevens squad trains in Kampala.

stories.title: Women's league expands to 14 clubs — and finally gets a title sponsor
stories.deck: The competition will play a full double round for the first time, with matches broadcast on radio.

body.text: The national women's league will expand to 14 clubs next season and play a full double round for the first time, backed by the competition's first title sponsor.
Clubs will receive a share of the sponsorship and support with travel, the single largest cost for teams outside the central region.
UnderCover Radio will carry a match of the week commentary.

stories.image_caption: Players warm up before a league fixture.

stories.title: The producer who turned boda horns into the song of the year
stories.deck: A field recording of Kampala traffic became the most recognisable hook of 2026. Its maker is still riding to the studio.

body.text: The hook arrives before the beat: two short horn blasts, a scooter engine, a distant conductor shouting a stage name. Then the bass drops, and the whole city seems to lean in.

The track, 'Kampala Anthem', was built from a morning of field recordings at a junction in Wandegeya. Its producer, 28, still rides a boda to the studio because parking in the city is worse than the traffic.
What makes the record work is not the novelty. It is the restraint: the horns are pitched, chopped and spaced so that the noise becomes rhythm rather than decoration.

text: Everybody hears the horns. Nobody listens to them. I just held the door open.

body.text: From the junction to the charts
Radio programmers were slow, then sudden. The song is now the most requested on three Kampala stations and has been licensed for a continental campaign.
The producer is wary of the follow-up. He has already recorded a follow-up of sorts: a market, at dawn, twelve minutes of tape, and no plan yet.

stories.image_caption: The artist performing the track live at a Kampala showcase.

stories.title: Kampala film festival returns with 40 screens and a local-first lineup
stories.deck: The programme is dominated by East African work, including six features making their debut in the city they were shot in.

body.text: The Kampala film festival opens next week across 40 screens, with a programme weighted toward East African features and documentaries.
Six films will have their first public screening in the city where they were shot, including a documentary about the market traders who rebuilt Kikuubo after the fire.
Organisers have added free daytime screenings for students, and a distribution market aimed at getting local films into regional cinemas.

stories.image_caption: Audiences at last year's opening night.

stories.title: Luganda pop is going global. The business is staying local.
stories.deck: Streaming has taken the sound abroad. The money, the rights and the management are still being worked out at home.

body.text: A year ago, a Luganda-language single could expect a few hundred thousand streams. This year, three have passed ten million, and the artists behind them have toured four continents.
The sound travels because it is specific: local slang, local rhythms, a cadence that does not need translation to work in a club in Nairobi or London.
The business has not travelled as well. Publishing splits are often informal, managers are sometimes cousins, and royalties are collected in currencies the artists cannot easily access.
The paperwork problem
Collecting societies say registration is improving, but a large share of the catalogue remains unregistered — which means money that is earned and never claimed.
The most successful artists are building teams: a lawyer, a manager, an accountant. That is less romantic than the sound, and probably more important to its survival.

stories.image_caption: A live set at the UnderCover Sessions.

stories.title: The week Kololo ran on colour: fashion in 24 frames
stories.deck: Backstage, on the runway and in the queue — the looks that defined the season's biggest showcase.

body.text: Four days, twenty-two designers and a queue that wrapped around the block: the season's showcase closed on Sunday with a sold-out finale.
Our photographers spent the week backstage and in the front row. These are the images that stayed with us.

stories.image_caption: A look from the closing show.

stories.title: Twenty years of the late-night voice that kept Kampala awake
stories.deck: From 10pm dedications to a podcast empire, the city's most enduring broadcaster on what changed and what did not.

body.text: At 9.50pm the studio lights dim, the microphone is checked twice, and the voice that has closed Kampala's day for two decades comes on air.
The format has barely changed: letters, requests, a caller who has had a difficult week. What changed is the audience, which now listens from four continents and sends messages in three languages.
The show's producer says the discipline is the same as it was in 2006: never rush a caller, never let a song do the talking when a person needs to.
Next year the programme becomes a daily podcast, a move the host describes — with some suspicion — as 'the same show, wearing a jacket'.

stories.image_caption: In the studio before a late-night broadcast.

stories.title: Streaming platforms commission their first Luganda-language series
stories.deck: Two productions will shoot in Kampala next year, with local crews and a share of the rights retained by the producers.

body.text: Two international streaming platforms have commissioned their first Luganda-language drama series, both to be shot in Kampala next year.
The deals are notable for what the producers kept: a share of the rights, and a commitment to local crews in senior roles.
Industry figures say the commissions are a test of whether the city can sustain year-round production, rather than the seasonal bursts it has relied on.

stories.image_caption: A set at a Kampala production studio.

stories.title: Our newsrooms must learn to listen
stories.deck: We are excellent at broadcasting and less good at hearing. That is a business problem as much as a democratic one.

body.text: There is a particular sound a newsroom makes when it is not listening: the confident tapping of a story that has already been decided.
We are good at broadcasting. We can fill three hours of airtime before lunch. What we are less good at is the slower work of hearing what an audience actually needs, as opposed to what it will click.
This is not only a democratic failing. It is a commercial one. Newspapers that do not hear their readers lose them quietly, long before the print run falls.

text: A listener is not an empty vessel. A listener is a source.

body.text: The fix is unglamorous: call people back, hold the microphone a beat longer, publish a corrections box that is easy to find, and ask the audience what we got wrong before they tell us with their feet.
UnderCover's radio desk has begun a weekly listening session in which four listeners critique the week's output. It is uncomfortable and cheap. Both are reasons to keep doing it.

stories.image_caption: Ruth Achieng writes The Long View every Thursday.

stories.title: The budget is not the problem. The plumbing is.
stories.deck: Every year we debate the number and ignore the pipes that decide whether it reaches a classroom.

body.text: Each June we argue about the size of the budget as though the number were the policy. It is not. A budget is a promise; the plumbing is what happens next.
Money that must pass through four approvals before it reaches a school is money that will be late, and often reduced. The delays are not accidents. They are the system working as designed.
The supplementary budget now before Parliament is a symptom. Fix the release cycle, publish the disbursement data monthly, and half the annual drama disappears.
None of this is exciting. It is, however, the difference between a statistic and a working clinic.

stories.image_caption: Daniel Okello is business editor.

stories.title: A city that works for the people who sell on its pavements
stories.deck: Kampala does not have a street trading problem. It has a market design problem.

body.text: The easiest thing to do about a pavement full of traders is to send an enforcement team. The hardest thing is to design a market they can afford to use.
For twenty years we have chosen the easy thing, and for twenty years the traders have come back. That is not stubbornness. It is economics.
A timed trading zone with a levy the vendor can actually pay would be a start. So would publishing the allocation of stalls, so that everyone can see who got one.
Cities are not tidy. A city that pretends otherwise just moves its untidiness out of sight.

stories.image_caption: Nakato Ssebunya is political editor.

stories.title: Sport is Uganda's cheapest diplomacy
stories.deck: One good tournament does more for the country's reputation than a year of consultants.

body.text: When the Cranes win, the country's name travels further than any trade delegation. When the athletes run, the flag appears in living rooms we could never buy into.
That is an extraordinary return on a modest investment, and yet sport remains the first line to be cut and the last to be planned.
Fund the facilities, pay the coaches, and let the federations run their competitions without interference. The rest follows.

stories.image_caption: Brian Kaggwa is sports editor.

stories.title: What the coffee boom should teach us about patience
stories.deck: Value is not created at the auction. It is created by the person who waits, and we have been slow to reward her.

body.text: A coffee tree takes three years to give its first real harvest and five to be worth the land it occupies. Nobody in the chain waits that long except the farmer.
Every record export year prompts a familiar conversation about branding and premium markets. The more useful conversation is about who carries the risk of the wait.
Cooperatives that pay a second payment after sale have shown what patience is worth when it is shared. The policy question is how to make that the norm rather than the exception.
